episodes.174199: After making landfall along the Florida Panhandle early on November 11th, the remnants of Tropical Storm Nicole progressed north toward far western North Carolina and Virginia. Moisture radiated well ahead of the storm, resulting in light rainfall during early morning hours, which gradually intensified as dawn approached and winds shifted from a east-northeast direction to become increasingly southeasterly by late morning. This direction is favorable for efficient orographic lift along the crest of the Blue Ridge with the southeasterly windflow tapping into deep moisture across the central Carolinas, where precipitable water values were measured in the 1.7 to 1.9 inch range.  Thirty-five to forty-five mph winds carried this moisture toward the mountains.  Rainfall rates for stations along the crest of the Blue Ridge, particularly in northwest North Carolina were observed in the 0.5 to 1 inch per hour range from around sunrise on the 11th until about 3 pm when winds began to shift more southwesterly.  Most significantly-impacted was the headwaters of the Watauga River, with significant flooding was observed along the river in the communities of Valle Crucis and Sugar Grove.
episodes.174833: Thunderstorms developed along a cold front that moved through South Central Texas. Some of these storms produced large hail.
episodes.174836: The remnants of Tropical Depression Nicole moved up through southern West Virginia on the evening of November 11th. Simultaneously, a cold front swept through the Ohio Valley and arrived into the state during the afternoon and evening hours, contributing to periods of moderate to heavy rainfall. Rain totals reached two inches in many parts of the state, but dry antecedent conditions allowed for the ground to soak up most of it and limited flooding potential. However, there was an instance of flash flooding within the city of Parkersburg along several intersections.
episodes.175232: Storms blossomed along a strong cold front and produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter across Bell and Lampasas counties.
episodes.175385: The remnants of Hurricane Nicole, in combination with a Great Lakes cold front, lead to heavy precipitation totals across the region.  Rainfall totals of 1.5 to 3.5 inches, with localized higher totals, were common across the region. Most of the rainfall falling during the November 11th calendar day.  However, flooding was limited to very isolated instances.  This was due to the quite dry antecedent conditions, as well as the relatively long 18 to 24 hour period during which the rain fell.
episodes.175386: The remnants of Hurricane Nicole, in combination with a Great Lakes cold front, lead to heavy precipitation totals across the region.  Rainfall totals of 1.5 to 3.5 inches, with localized higher totals, were common across the region. Most of the rainfall falling during the November 11th calendar day.  However, flooding was limited to very isolated instances.  This was due to the quite dry antecedent conditions, as well as the relatively long 18 to 24 hour period during which the rain fell.
episodes.175614: During the late morning into the afternoon, the remnants of Tropical Storm Nicole moved across far western North Carolina and far southwest Virginia. To the east of this system, a southeast wind ushered in warm and unstable air into the Virginia Southside. This allowed scattered showers and thunderstorms to develop. One of these storms downed a couple of trees in Henry County. Outside of the storms, gusty southeast winds and a moist ground contributed to at least four additional trees falling in Henry County.
episodes.175685: A combination of Tropical Depression Nicole and the approach of a cold front caused scattered severe thunderstorms which produced damaging winds and two tornadoes across portions of central and south central Virginia.
episodes.175686: A combination of Tropical Depression Nicole and the approach of a cold front caused scattered thunderstorms which produced heavy rain which caused flash flooding across portions of central Virginia.
episodes.175707: A cold front moved through the region during the evening of the 11th with scattered thunderstorms. One storm became severe in Southeast Texas.
episodes.175838: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms moved across portions of the South Carolina coastal waters within the broad circulation around Tropical Depression Nicole which was centered near the Florida panhandle. A few of the thunderstorms produced strong wind gusts.
episodes.175891: Unseasonably high moisture interacted with a stationary, weakening frontal boundary to produce heavy rainfall across western North Carolina throughout the 11th. Flash flooding developed along several basins across the northern mountains after 4 to 7 inches of rain fell in around 24 hours, with roughly half of that falling within a few hours during the morning.

The Watauga River at Sugar Grove (SGWN7) crested at 13.01 feet 5:15 pm EST on Nov 11th due to prolonged moderate to heavy rain associated with the remnants of Tropical Storm Nicole.  This is the 20th-highest crest in the history of this gage, and is the highest crest since June 2019. This crest (8,630 cfs) ranks between a 2-year and a 5-year event (0.5-0.2 ARI) per USGS StreamStats.
Reported via mPing.
Hail up to half dollar was reported within the Killeen city limits.
Golf ball sized hail was reported on FM 2484 to the west of FM 1620 near Salado.
Reported via mPing.
Two inch sized hail was reported, and the hail cracked a windshield.

The Middle Fork South Fork of the New River at Deerfield Road crested at 6.92 feet at 11 am on the 11th and remained above 6.5 feet into late afternoon. This stream overflowed its banks across Deerfield Road.
The Dewitt Barnett Road bridge crossing the Watauga River was submerged at least 2 feet deep by flooding.  No damage was reported and the bridge reopened after flooding subsided.

County comms and stream gauges indicated flash flooding developed across Avery County after 4 to 7 inches of rain fell across the eastern half of the county in around 24 hours, with 1 to 2 inches of that falling in a couple of hours during the late morning and early afternoon. Multiple roads were closed due to high water including Greene Rd and Puckett Rd (due to flooding along the Elk River). Multiple other streams were impacted in the Banner Elk area, where at least one building was surrounded by floodwater. A stream gauge on the North Toe River in Newland also exceeded its established flood stage indicating inundation of Linville St.

County comms reported flash flooding developed along the Ostin Creek basin after 3 to 4 inches of rain fell in around 24 hours, with around half of that falling during the late morning. Holbert Cove Rd was inundated and closed in at least one spot.
Spotter reported a funnel cloud north of Lawrenceville.

County comms reported flash flooding developed along the Brushy Creek basin after 5 to 7 inches of rain fell across the basin in around 24 hours, with 1 to 2 inches of that falling in just a couple of hours centered around noon. Inundation across Estattoe Acres Way forced evacuation of a mobile home community.
Thunderstorm winds blew down one large tree which blocked one lane on Preston Road near the intersection of Wingfield Orchard Road.
A thunderstorm produced hail ranging from pea to nickel size in Lakeway. Most of the hail was pea size.

A cell phone video from a motorist in the Valle Crusis area showed Dutch Creek and a smaller creek (name unknown) that runs along Frank Mast Road both out of their banks.  Water from these flooded creeks was observed up against the Valle Crucis United Methodist Church, the Valle Crucis Log Cabin Rentals, and the Mast General Store.  Portions of the Valle Crusis Community Park was flooded over a foot deep.  Water was observed flowing across Broadstone Road.  Reported damage was minor and consisted mainly of cleanup of debris.

Flooding from Dutch Creek flooded the property of Valle Crucis Elementary School all the way up to the school building. Water did enter portions of the building, but cleanup was quick and no damage was reported in the building.  Cleanup of the school grounds consisted mainly of debris removal.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a pine tree across the 300 block of Boat Dock Road.

A cell phone video showed the Watauga River flowing over a foot deep across Guy Ford Road in western Watauga County during the afternoon of November 11th. Large debris was caught on the bridge that would require equipment for removal.
Multiple pictures of a funnel cloud were reported south of downtown Richmond.
Flash flooding was reported at Interstate 95 and Belvidere Street. The shoulder and left lane were closed.
Multiple spotters reported a funnel cloud near Waverly.
Tree was downed at the intersection of Studley Road and Shelton Pointe Drive.
Funnel cloud was reported.

An EF0 tornado touched down briefly in northern King and Queen County south of Root Swamp Road. The tornado tracked north along north Root Swamp Road uprooting trees and snapping tree limbs. The tornado then tracked into Caroline county.

An EF0 tornado tracked from King and Queen county into Caroline county. The tornado struck a farm in Tignor at the intersection of Sparta Road and Tignor Road (Root Swamp Road becomes Tignor Road). Several outbuildings were heavily damaged or destroyed. One silo was damaged along with 3 tractors. The tornado dissipated just north of the farm.
The South Fork of the New River at M.L.K. Jr. Street in the Town of Boone crested at 12.07 feet.

The EF0 tornado in Dinwiddie county was confirmed partially via drone footage from a storm chaser positioned along Route 40 as the storm tracked north. The video showed a funnel reaching the ground and a brief period of debris just north of Route 40. NWS storm survey found a snapped cedar tree and broken limbs along Ridge Road just south|of Route 40. Much of the area is highly wooded and inaccessible. Damage was all very light with winds estimated around 50 to 55 mph.

The East Fork South Fork of the New River at Deerfield Road crested at 7.94 feet at 4 pm on the 11th.  This stream overflowed its banks several inches deep across both Deerfield Road and Bamboo Road further upstream.  Remediation consisted of only minor debris removal.

County comms reported flash flooding developed along Wilson Creek after 4 to 6 inches of rain fell over the headwaters in around 24 hours, with 1 to 2 inches of that falling during the early afternoon of the 11th. At least one road was inundated (Brown Mountain Beach Rd). One person had to be rescued after being isolated by floodwater.

A stream gauge on Johns River in Burke County exceeded its established flood stage, indicating flooding along the river upstream in Caldwell County after 4 to 7 inches of rain fell in the basin in about 24 hours. Highway 90 and Adako Rd were inundated in the Collettsville community.

A stream gauge on the Johns River north of Morganton exceeded its established flood stage after 4 to 7 inches of rain fell in the basin, including the Wilson Creek tributary during the morning of the 11th. Flooded roads included Johns River Loop Rd, Old Johns River Rd, and Valley View Cir. A few campgrounds along the river and its smaller tributaries were also flooded.

Flooding was observed in multiple areas within Parkersburg, including the intersection of Camden Avenue and Division Street, as well as spots along Stillwell Road, Chesterville Road, Knobs Hill Road, and College Parkway.
Wind gusts downed multiple trees around the town of Burkeville.
